messages.author: 0ed14b8ed63cf572
messages.subject: Multivariate ordered logistic model not converging
parts:
I am trying to model ordinal data from a survey as a multivariate ordered logistic model. I am finding that as I increase the number of questions in the data (from 10 items to 16 items), the chains do not converge. The output for all of the chains in the 10 item dataset show convergence, but for the 16 item dataset, only 1 of the chains converge. 

The underlying latent parameter for the questions are modelled as a multivariate normal distribution, and each integer response as an ordered logistic. I am modelling the prior for the cutpoints for each item as a fixed-scaled cumulative sum of a symmetric dirichlet. For identifiability, I set the first cutpoint to 0. I am running on CmdStan (v2.4), Linux Ubuntu.

Do you have any suggestions for choices of priors or scales that might help convergence? My eventual goal is to include all the data, which is 56 questions.

Hi Kevin,

I am also modeling a ordered logistic with Stan. What brought you to set the cut points' prior as fixed-scaled cumulative sum of a dirichlet? How different are the results comparing with a non-informative prior on cut points by not specifying anything?

My model might also has the identificability issue given that intercept is included. The cut points and intercepts might run into each other. But I am not sure because I am modeling the intercept as a random effect. As shown in my model below, do I also need to specify priors for muAlpha and sigmaAlpha?

code <- '  // STAN: hierarchical ordered logistic model

  real muAlpha;  // mu for intercept

  real beta1;  // slope for sex
  real beta2;  // slope for age
  ordered[K-1] c;  // cutpoints for ordered logistic model

transformed parameters {
  vector[N] y_hat;
  for (n in 1:N)
    y_hat[n] <- alpha[group[n]] + beta1 * sex[n] + beta2 * age[n];
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(muAlpha, sigmaAlpha);  // intercept
  /* priors for muAlpha, sigmaAlpha, c can be further specified */

  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(y_hat[n], c);
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] loglik;

    loglik[n] <- ordered_logistic_log(y[n], y_hat[n], c);

messages.subject: Re: Multivariate ordered logistic model not converging
parts:
I got the idea for setting the cut point prior as fixed-scaled cumulative sum of a dirichlet from this thread:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/2YMo3SUzHTg/jgeoyZfUSBsJ

When the cutpoints have a non-informative prior, I found it was extremely slow to converge (over 10 times as long) versus setting a more informative prior. However, looking at the older thread, the poster seems to have convergence issues as well in some of the chains with this approach.

I'm definitely not an expert, but I have found that constraining the prior helps with non-identifiability issues and convergence speed. You might want to put a broad prior, even a normal(0,10) or cauchy(0,10) (for longer tails) on muAlpha and sigmaAlpha.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multivariate ordered logistic model not converging
parts:
We don't (yet) have any default recommendations for priors on
cutpoints.

The main issue you have to deal with is making sure you
don't have multiplicative (scale) or additive (location)
identifiability issues with the cutpoints and a regression.

If you give the regression a mean and the cutpoints float,
then you have a classic non-identifiability problem. You
can pin the value of one of the cutpoints to identify the
location. Then if you still need to worry about identifying
the scales.

- Bob

parts:
Three suggestions.

1. You don't need to save yHat as a transformed parameter if you don't
need it in the output. You can make it a local variable in the model.
Then you'd have to recompute it in the generated quantities block, but
you can also do that as a local variable. Then you don't output yHat.

2. You don't want to try to set c[k] to cu[k] - cu[1]. That doesn't
identify the cu because they can all shift and you get the same behavior.
Instead, do something like declaring cu as pos_ordered[K-2], then setting
c[1] to 0, and all c[k] to cu[k-1].

3. You can use the non-centered parameterization for alpha. Define
alpha_raw ~ normal(0,1) and then define alpha <- muAlpha + sigma_alpha * alpha_raw.
This is much faster when there's not much data to estimate alpha with.
It may not matter here if alpha is well identified by the model.

- Bob

Three suggestions.

- Bob

The variables with scope over the blocks are saved. That
means in the transformed data, transformed parameters, and generated
quantities block, the initial sequence of variable declarations are
the ones that are saved.

For ones you don't want to save, you can make a local block
using curly braces. For example, in

generated quantities {
real gq_scope;
{
real local_scope;
... use either var ...
}
... only use gq_scope ...
}

the variable "gq_scope" scopes over the entire generated quantities
block, whereas the variable local_scope declared inside curly braces
can only be used inside those braces and won't be saved.

- Bob
